intro: Eugen d’Albert recorded this Nocturne in 1916. In a recollection reproduced by Mark Mitchell and Allan Evans, Wilhelm Kempff describes d’Albert making a sustained note seem to sing and changing the colour of a repeated phrase. That testimony offers a specific listening question, not a claim that a piano can produce a singer’s continuous vibrato.
question: How much can the apparent colour of a repeated melody change without changing its notes?

sections.label: A′ · Larghetto returns
sections.mNote: the opening song returns after the faster middle

cues.title: A sustained line on piano
cues.text: The opening asks a struck instrument to sustain a singing phrase. Listen to the relation between long melody notes and the accompaniment beneath them; the surrounding attacks help determine how continuous the line seems.
cues.evidence: Opening melody and accompaniment: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173. The invitation concerns the score’s texture, not an inferred recording technique.

cues.title: A pupil of Liszt
cues.text: D’Albert studied with Liszt in Weimar from 1882. That relationship is part of his training, but it does not make this 1916 record a direct document of how Liszt or Chopin played the Nocturne.
cues.evidence: Mark Mitchell and Allan Evans, The Centaur Pianist notes: https://arbiterrecords.org/catalog/eugen-d-albert-the-centaur-pianist/

cues.title: A documented old disc
cues.text: The source identifies a 1916 Gramophone recording with matrix 1120m. Its original catalogue number is inconsistent between the item text and the pictured CD track list; the dossier preserves that disagreement rather than silently choosing one.
cues.evidence: Archive item identifies045678 while its track-list scan prints045578; both give1120m/1916: https://archive.org/metadata/02-eugen-d-albert-syposium-1146 and https://archive.org/download/02-eugen-d-albert-syposium-1146/D%27Albert%20tracks.jpg

cues.title: The inner motion changes
cues.text: The faster middle is marked doppio movimento. It starts with a subdued character and develops more force; following the growth is more informative than hearing the entire contrasting section as one loud block.
cues.evidence: Approximate report boundary1:28 precedes the rise towards1:35–1:45. Markings and central trajectory: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Kempff’s account of colour
cues.text: Kempff described d’Albert’s sustained note as giving an illusion of human vibrato, followed by a different tone colour on a repeated phrase. This is a musician’s account of expressive effect, not a measurement of the piano string’s pitch.
cues.evidence: Kempff’s memoir account, specifically introduced in discussion of this Nocturne, is reproduced in the Arbiter notes: https://arbiterrecords.org/catalog/eugen-d-albert-the-centaur-pianist/. The notes concern the historical performance, not the selected Symposium transfer’s processing.

cues.title: The song returns
cues.text: The slower opening material comes back after the central surge. Listen for the continuity of the melodic line through its decorations; compare the return’s balance and pacing with the beginning without expecting mechanically identical phrasing.
cues.evidence: Approximate return around2:04, following low-level windows at1:55–2:00. Reprise form: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A colour is a relation
cues.text: On a piano, a change of apparent colour can involve the strength, spacing and overlap of attacks around a melody. Use Kempff’s account as a question to test while listening, not as proof of a particular touch or pedal movement here.
cues.evidence: Listening invitation motivated by the documented Kempff account in https://arbiterrecords.org/catalog/eugen-d-albert-the-centaur-pianist/. No physical performance technique is inferred from this transfer.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

transitions.title: The singing phrase yields to doubled motion
transitions.how: The opening’s ornamented song is interrupted by the faster central texture. The doppio movimento marking changes the scale of motion, while sotto voce leaves space for the passage to grow. This contrast is built into the score and should not be mistaken for an undocumented speed change in the transfer.
transitions.evidence: Approximate report boundary1:28; ensuing rise to the1:35–1:45 crest. Score markings: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173

transitions.title: The middle’s activity subsides into a reprise
transitions.how: The concentrated middle withdraws and the slower melodic texture returns. The theme can now be recognised against the central episode’s greater density. D’Albert’s expressive balance remains a listening question; the formal return itself does not establish how he produced a particular colour.
transitions.evidence: Estimated return after the lower-level1:55–2:00 windows, around2:04. Reprise function: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173

facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
